title: Don't Trouble the Trouble
dek: A strange little fantasy that works better when you think like a child than when you question it like an adult.
review: Don't Trouble the Trouble begins with an idea that is a little removed from reality, but that is also where its charm starts. The first half is engaging, the second half is reasonably watchable, and the climax works well enough without turning the film into something bigger than it really is.

Fahadh Faasil is the film's biggest strength. He does not need exaggerated hero moments to hold attention; his reactions, timing and ability to stay natural inside an unusual situation give the movie its personality. The child artist is excellent. Her innocence is crucial because the story becomes more interesting when we see the world through a child who cannot always separate what is real from what might be magic.

That childlike uncertainty is probably the film's most appealing idea. Adults immediately try to explain everything. A child can simply accept the possibility that something impossible may be true. If there is still a little child and a little wonder left in you, the movie becomes easier to enjoy.

The screenplay, however, leaves some obvious entertainment unused. Once the hero is connected to a supernatural presence, the audience naturally expects him to discover clever or funny ways to benefit from it. The film does not really exploit that possibility. At first that feels disappointing. At the same time, there is something respectable about not reducing the supernatural element to a convenient machine that solves the hero's problems.

The villain track mainly exists to push the hero's journey forward. It does not add enough on its own, and stronger antagonists could have made the film more gripping. The hero's friend character works better and brings some welcome ease. Subbaraju and the supporting cast perform their parts well.

The film also benefits from its Hyderabad flavour. The locations give the fantasy a grounded texture instead of making everything feel like an anonymous studio world. Technically the movie is solid. The visuals are clean, the effects are sufficient for the story and the music supports the film, even if it is not something I carried out of the theatre.

There is no conventional heroine track and the film does not depend on songs to keep restarting the audience's attention. Still, it remains engaging for most of its runtime. More comedy and tighter writing could have made it considerably stronger.

The concept is not completely unprecedented. A few ideas may remind you of older fantasy films, but the director manages to twist familiar ingredients enough to create his own version. It is not a never-before-seen concept, yet it does not feel like a lazy copy either.

My biggest confusion after the film was the title itself. Why exactly is it called Don't Trouble the Trouble? You can think about the characters and construct an interpretation, but the connection between the title and the screenplay is not immediately satisfying.

Overall, this is good cinema rather than a must-watch theatrical event. Fahadh gives it personality, the child performance gives it innocence, and the central fantasy gives it enough freshness to stay watchable. If you have time this weekend, go with a child's mindset and you may have a pleasant time. If not, it is also perfectly reasonable to catch it later on OTT.
works: Fahadh Faasil, the excellent child performance, the central childlike fantasy, Hyderabad flavour, clean technical work and an engaging first half.
misses: Underused supernatural possibilities, a weak villain track, room for more comedy, uneven second-half grip and a title whose connection to the story remains unclear.
